notes.text: I'm going to begin by reading the mission briefing.

I'm weighing how to use the 10 test drops. Each one gives an impact point, a fall time, whether it entered smoke, and a noisy wind reading at its own altitude. The wind measured at the aircraft's altitude is one data point, but shear and veer still need drops at other altitudes to pin down. I'm starting to think about how fall time depends on altitude, mostly through gravity.

I'm working out how fall time shrinks with altitude, mostly from gravity with some drag, so a 100 m drop takes about 4.5 seconds. Wind pushes the load sideways by wind times that fall time, and drag pulls it toward the air's velocity. Since a drop at high altitude reveals more about shear, I'm planning to spread the test drops across different altitudes.

I'm now settling on the test drop plan: one at 150 m, one at 30 m, and maybe one at 100 m, so the measured winds at those altitudes reveal shear and veer. I'm also weighing how to handle drag from the fall-time readings, and I'll pick a 90-degree heading at 60 m/s, keeping the release point clear of the smoke so the updraft doesn't skew the calibration.

I'm settling on a first test drop at x=-300, heading 90 at 150 m altitude, since a release that far from the smoke should keep the load clear while still giving a wind reading aloft.

I'm working out the drop: 150 m height gives a fall time of about 10.9 s, and the load lands 133 m east of the release point with the aircraft moving at 60 m/s. Without drag the fall would take only about 5.5 s, so air resistance must be large, and I'm starting to consider how quadratic drag would limit the fall speed.

Now I'm checking the drag numbers against the fall times: a terminal speed near 11 m/s for a drag coefficient around 0.08, and a second drop that implies a k below 0.12. For the horizontal motion, the load averages about 20.7 m/s over its 3.3 s fall, so drag must be pulling it down from 60 m/s quickly toward the air speed. I'm about to work through the first drop's horizontal displacement the same way.

Now I'm working out the average horizontal speed for the first drop, about 12.2 m/s, and noting the wind at 150 m is about 7.6 m/s. I'm also trying to pin down the wind at 100 m by fitting a power-law profile to the two measured levels, which gives an exponent near 0.25, though the noise in those readings leaves the shear uncertain.

I'm fitting the wind direction from the two measured levels, which gives roughly 92° and a small veer, though the 4° noise makes that loose. Since the wind is nearly all easterly, I'm thinking about adding drops in other directions to pin down the direction better.

I'm weighing which measurement would tell me the most: a drop at 100 m, approached from a different heading, to pin down the wind there, and a drop through smoke to check for an updraft. The rest of the unknowns, drag, wind speed, direction, shear and veer, can be refined afterward by comparing simulated trajectories with the measured ones.

I'm weighing a second drop at 100 m with a northward heading to test how heading shapes the horizontal drift, and I'm also considering a drop through the smoke column to check for an updraft.

I'm planning a drop through the smoke column: releasing from roughly x = -150 m at 100 m altitude, the load should drift east through the fire's center. Updraft from the smoke would lengthen the fall, which I can read from the fall time.

I'm planning a test drop at 100 m altitude from x = -150 m heading east, so the load crosses the fire's center and I can read both the wind at that height and any updraft from the fall time. Once I have that, I'll compare the other unknowns against the target drops, since the smoke columns there will also shift the fall.

I'm weighing whether the updraft from the target's smoke will stretch the fall enough to shift the drift, and I'll need an estimate of it. For now I'm settling on two more test drops: one at 100 m altitude heading east from x = -150 m so the load passes through the smoke, and one heading north to pin down the wind direction at that height.

The wind at 100 m reads about 6.8 at 94°, which fits the power-law estimate. The smoke-entry fall time is 7.73 s, between the 3.32 s for 30 m and the 10.9 s for 150 m. Next I'll fit drag and updraft, starting from a test with drag 0.05 and wind 6.

I'm running a few comparisons with different drag values, holding the wind at about 6.8 from 93° with the shear, veer, and updraft settings fixed, and checking the predicted fall times against the three observed drops.

I'm wondering why updraft 5 made no difference in the comparison with drop 3, since the rows came out identical. The updraft should reach drop 3 because it entered the smoke, so I'm checking whether the comparison applies the updraft at all or whether the match is just a coincidence, though an exact match to zero seems unlikely.

I'm checking the rows for drop 3 with updraft 5 against updraft 0, since both drag-0.06 calls returned identical numbers. Given the smoke path and the updraft strength, the difference should be noticeable, so I'm going to look at whether the compare tool applies the updraft at all.

I'm now checking the drag fit: at drag 0.04 the predicted fall times run about 0.1 to 0.2 s longer than observed, which suggests more drag is needed, but the drag 0.06 result for test 1 looks inconsistent with that direction, so I'm rechecking the sign of the residual.

I'm noticing that a higher drag should shorten the fall, yet the drag 0.06 residual grew to 2.14 instead of shrinking, which doesn't fit the physics. Either the updraft 0 call is off somehow, or I'm misreading the sign of the difference, so I'm going to recheck which call corresponds to which setting.

I had drag backwards: higher drag slows the fall, so the longer predicted times mean I should try a slightly lower drag, around 0.035. The horizontal residuals point the other way, with the predicted x falling short of observed, so the fit needs more eastward travel as well.

I'm testing drag values of 0.035 and 0.038 with the wind held constant, since the positive timing residuals at 0.04 suggest the fall is still slightly too slow. I'll also rerun the updraft 5 case at drag 0.04 to see whether it changes the drop 3 result.

I'm checking how much the updraft changes the result for drop 3: a drag of 0.04 with updraft 5 gives 0.23 s against 0.22 s with no updraft. That's only about a 0.01 s difference, which seems small for a load that drops through the smoke region, so I'm wondering whether the updraft's effect is smaller than I expected.

The updraft's effect still looks too small for a 5 m/s updraft over several seconds, so I'm suspecting it isn't being applied in the comparison. I'll run a simulation of a drop that clearly passes through the smoke, with updraft 0 and then 5, to see whether the fall time actually changes.

The impact point for drop 3 sits at x=-41.8, just inside the smoke edge, and the load only reaches the smoke near the ground. Since the updraft factor min(1, z/15) is small there, its effect on this drop is naturally tiny, so drop 3 is a weak test. I'll design a cleaner check: a drop from about 150 m with the release set so the path crosses the fire center at mid altitude, where the updraft is at full strength.

I'm going to simulate a drop from 150 m with the release set so the load crosses the fire center at mid altitude, where the updraft is at full strength. I'll run it with updraft 10 and with updraft 0 to compare impact points and fall times. A strong updraft should lengthen the fall noticeably, so if drop 3 showed almost no change, the updraft may simply have been weak near the ground there.

I'm going to run a simulation of a designed drop to test how sensitive the fall time is to the updraft.

The updraft 10 run shows a large effect, with fall time 16.3 against 10.7, so the sensor should pick it up clearly. Drop 3 told me little because it landed near the ground. A calibration drop at altitude 150 through the smoke should reveal the updraft far better, so I'll run it at x=-130, y=0, heading 90, speed 60, expecting an impact around x=3.4 with updraft 0. That drop would also check the wind.

I'm weighing whether the updraft could also bend this drop's path near the fire center, which would muddy the calibration, though I think the run will still be informative.

The observed fall time of 12.25 seconds is about 1.5 seconds longer than the no-updraft case, so there's clearly an updraft acting. The impact figure of 8.6 also falls between the predictions for no updraft and a 10 m/s updraft, which points to a updraft somewhere around 2 to 3 m/s. I'll run the comparison across all four drops with updraft values of 2.5 and 3, keeping drag at 0.036.

I'm also noting that the wind at 150 reads 7.7 at 88° this time, a bit noisy against the earlier 7.6 at 91°. Next I'll run the comparison for updraft values of 2, 3, and 4.

I'm checking the drop 4 numbers at updraft 3.5, where the predicted time is short of the observed one by 0.35. Extrapolating the trend from the two updraft values suggests the zero point sits near 4.4, so I'll test 4.5 next. The horizontal residual looks like it crosses zero closer to 3.

I'm also weighing the drag variations, since the drop 1-3 residuals run slightly negative at drag 0.036. Next I'll try updraft values of 4.5 and 4.0.

I'm checking the updraft fit: the time offset comes out near zero, but the horizontal offset for drop 4 is off by more than the noise, and the prediction runs too far east at higher updraft.

The updraft and drag suggest the residuals don't agree: the time fit wants about 4.4 and the horizontal drift wants about 2.7. Since they can't both hold, I'm starting to think wind speed, shear, or drag has to take up the slack, and I'd want more data near the smoke at a different altitude to tell updraft and shear apart.

Still weighing whether the load passes through the smoke, which it will since we drop at the target. The remaining six drops need to separate drag from wind, so I'm planning headings that change the relative velocity, plus a test well away from the smoke at 100 m with the aircraft flying north at 60 to see the drift.

I'm settling on a sixth test: a southbound pass at 60 m, 45 knots, placed well off to the side of the smoke, then a westward-facing run at some altitude to check the drift in another direction.

Now I'm comparing the observed impact point with the release point, and the northward shift works out to about 61 m, with an eastward offset of 44.1 m. The earlier drag-free estimate was far larger, so I'm checking that drag explains the gap.

The fall time of 7.8 s at 100 m matches the earlier 7.73 s drop, though that one had an updraft from smoke and this one doesn't, so the drag estimate looks plausible. I'm now weighing a drag coefficient of 0.036 against the measured wind of about 6.8 m/s at 94 m, which averages near 7.1 m/s at 92.5 m, and checking whether the 4.2 m/s updraft hypothesis fits better.

I'm checking the drop 4 x-residual of +5.4 against the wind there, which I estimate near 7.8 at about 91° after applying the shear to the surface wind.

I'm comparing the 5.4 drop 4 x-residual against the wind there, which I estimate at about 7.8 at 91° after applying the shear. The gap is either the wind at 150 running slightly too strong or an updraft issue. I'd rather fit the parameters systematically than guess, since the compare tool is the only evaluator and I have plenty of calcs left to search with.

I'm comparing the drop 1, 2 and 4 x-residuals, all at or near the 150 m layer, against the predicted wind there. The y-residuals for drops 1 and 2 lean the same way, which points to the wind direction being slightly off rather than just speed. I'm going to try lowering the wind speed at 150 m by adjusting the shear.

I'm fitting the wind speed profile against the observed speeds at 30, 100 and 150 m. A shear exponent near 0.15 fits the 150 m speeds better, but it overshoots the 30 m observation, so I'm weighing which of the two to trust more.

I'm checking whether the x-residuals at 150 m point to the wind there running too strong, or to the updraft being off. Raising the updraft would push the predicted drift further east, but it would also make the fall time disagree with the observed one.

I'm weighing whether a lower drag would help the drop 4 x-residual, since less drag means less slowing in the horizontal direction and so more eastward drift.

I'm weighing whether a lower drag or a lower updraft would close the drop 4 x-gap, since higher drag cuts the eastward drift but lengthens the fall time. The two effects pull against each other, so I'm considering solving for drag and updraft together instead of adjusting one at a time.

I'm going to run three compares with different combinations of drag, wind speed, and updraft, all keeping direction at 92 and shear at 0.25, to see which one closes the drop 4 x-gap.

I'm checking how the wind speed affects the horizontal drift of drops 4 and 5, since drop 5 moves north and is sensitive to the wind at 100 m. A change from 6.6 to 7.1 m/s shifts its drift by roughly 4 m, so the W value matters a lot here.

I'm comparing four parameter combinations and tabulating the horizontal and vertical drift and time residuals for each drop. Drop 5's vertical drift swings a lot between them, so the drag value looks like the main driver there.

I'm working out the sum of squared residuals for each combination, treating the drag, wind, and drift values as noisy around a 1.5 m per-axis error. The first combination comes to roughly 52.5 across the position residuals, which works out to about 23 per value over the ten values.

I'm running the same sum-of-squares check on drops 4 and 5 for the other candidate sets, and the totals come out near 38 to 40 across 15 measurements, well above the expected ~15, so none of them fits especially well yet. The hypothesis with the lowest drop 4 and drop 5 residuals is still the one I'm weighing most heavily.

I'm checking whether the drop 4 timing residual is what's pushing the H_C fit up, since its 0.39 s mismatch dominates the total. For H1 the drop 4 horizontal residual is the biggest term instead. That points to the model possibly missing wind shear or veer at 150 m, so I'm looking at how the observed winds at 30, 100, and 150 m might be shaping drop 4's drift.

I'm checking the wind readings at 100 and 150 m: the 100 m values from drops 3 and 5 average about 7.1 m/s, and the 150 m values about 7.65 m/s. From those I'm estimating the shear exponent to be roughly 0.2, and I'm now looking at whether the wind direction veers with height.

I'm checking the wind direction at each height, which averages to about 93° near 30 m, 92.7° at 100 m, and 89.5° at 150 m. That suggests the wind veers slightly as altitude increases, roughly −3° per 100 m with a base direction near 91°, though the 4° noise per measurement keeps that estimate weak.

I'm weighing whether a drag increase of about 0.002 could explain drop 4's horizontal residual, since the sensitivity there is roughly -1.4 m. Before settling on this, I'm considering whether another drop at a different altitude would pin down updraft and drag better, and I'm noting that all five remaining test drops could go to calibration.

I'm now planning a sixth test drop: heading 180 at about 50 m altitude and 80 m/s, released north of the fire, to check how drag scales with speed and heading.

I'm weighing whether a sixth test drop would separate updraft from drag better than the smoke drops, and I'm settling on heading 180 at about 60 m altitude and 80 m/s, released from 200 m north of the fire to check how drag scales with speed.

Drop 6 checks out: the drop fell 67.4 m over 5.49 s with a horizontal offset of 23.9 m, and the wind at 60 m was 6.7 at 93 m, which the power-law estimate of 6.25 roughly matches. Next I'll set it against H1 and H_D.

I'm checking the drop 6 vertical residual, which is -3.3 m, meaning the prediction ended up 3.3 m south of the observed position. Drop 6 actually moved 67 m south, and comparing drag values, 0.039 looks like the best fit.

I'm working through the drop 4 and drop 1 residuals against the drag values, and the no-smoke drops mostly point to a drag coefficient around 0.038.

I'm now checking how drop 4's time residual depends on the updraft and drag together. Going from drag 0.036 to 0.038 shifts the drop 4 time residual by about +0.29 s, so the updraft has to come down to keep it near zero.

I'm working out the updraft for drop 4 at drag 0.038: a time residual of +0.39 s means the prediction runs long, and since a larger updraft lengthens the fall, the updraft needs to come down to roughly 3.6.

Checking the updraft against drop 4's time residual, I need to bring it down from 4.5 to around 3.6 to offset the extra drag. That lower updraft should also pull the drop 4 horizontal residual closer to zero. The combination I'm leaning toward is drag 0.038, wind 7.0, direction 92, shear 0.25, veer -2, and updraft 3.6, and I still need to check what that does to the drop 6 vertical residual.

The drop 6 vertical residual at drag 0.038 works out to about -0.75 m, which is close enough to zero to confirm that value.

I'm checking the current best fit: d=0.038, W=7.0, u=3.6, with residuals that look fairly small. The y residuals are mostly negative, averaging about -1.4, so the prediction runs consistently low on that axis.

I'm checking whether the wind direction could explain the consistent negative y residuals, since a slight change in the assumed direction would shift the predicted north position by about 1.7 m over the drop. The measured wind directions average around 91.7, though, which would point the other way, so that explanation doesn't quite hold up.

The fit residuals all lean negative in y, so I'm checking whether a wind direction shift could account for it. A northward push would need the wind somewhat below 90 degrees, but the measured directions sit near 92, which points the wrong way, so I'm looking at other possible sources of the bias, like a veer in the wind profile at altitude.

The mean y residual of about -1.4 is small against the 6 m accuracy target, but I'm checking whether drag on the north-heading drop could be driving drop 5's larger -2.3 residual. Drop 6 comes in at only -0.7, so the heading-dependent drag idea doesn't clearly explain the pattern either.

Checking whether a wind direction change near 89 or 90 degrees would center the y residuals, since it's the cheapest hypothesis left to test.

I'm working through the residuals for wind direction 89 and 92, where 89 pushes the mean positive and 92 pushes it negative. Interpolating puts the zero crossing near 90.5 degrees, and each 3-degree change moves the mean dy by about 2.4 m. Now I'm checking whether the veer through the column changes that estimate at 100 m.

Comparing the veer -2 and veer -6 cases, the mean dy shifts by about 0.5 m, so veer has a small effect at this height. Wind direction around 90.5 degrees sits within one standard error of the measured mean of about 91.7 degrees, so I'll keep it. Next I'm checking the dx residuals, which average around +0.3 and look fine, and I'll compare the final parameter set against the data.

The fit residuals look fine: the x and y offsets average out small, and the time residuals are negligible, so the scatter is within the noise I'd expect. Four test drops are still left, and the open questions are shear and veer, which I suspect come mostly from wind at other altitudes, along with the updraft.

I'm now weighing the updraft more carefully, since the only real smoke data comes from drop 4 at altitude 150. Targets should have intensities between 0.5 and 1.4, so I'm treating the updraft as scaling with intensity and the smoke radius as growing with its square root. Whether a drop lands inside the smoke depends on the trajectory through it, which in turn depends on release altitude and timing.

I'm going to test the updraft at a lower altitude, around 60 to 80 meters, with a slower drop so the load passes through the smoke closer to the ground. I'll simulate the predicted impact with the updraft at its fitted strength and again with it set to zero to see how much it changes the result.

The updraft shows up clearly here, with a 0.84 s time difference and a 4 m horizontal shift, so this drop is a usable measurement. I'll run test 7 from (-90, 0) heading 90 at 80 m altitude and 50 speed to check the updraft effect at that height.

I'm comparing the observed and predicted values for dt and dx: dt is off by about 0.07, and dx is off by 2.4 in the predicted-minus-observed direction, which is reasonable. The updraft value of 3.6 checks out, and I still need to compare everything against all seven.

I'm settling on a shear of 0.25, since 0.1 biases the dx residual positive and 0.4 biases it negative. I'll also check 0.2 later on.

I'm checking whether the veer is actually worth constraining, since a 3-degree direction error over a ~10 s fall could shift the landing point by several metres. The measured directions already show a slight drift with altitude, from about 93 degrees low down to around 89.5 at 150 m, so I'll use the last three drops to pin that down.

I'm fitting a line to the direction-versus-altitude points to estimate the veer, which comes out to roughly -3 degrees per 100 m.

I'm running the regression on the direction data: the slope comes out to about -0.033 degrees per metre, so the veer is roughly -3.3 degrees per 100 m. That puts the direction at 100 m near 91.7 degrees, which doesn't quite match the 90.5 from the earlier fit that assumed a veer of -2.

Checking the veer estimate: the slope SE works out to about ±3.7 degrees per 100 m, so the value is only loosely pinned. Two more drops, one at 30 m and one at 150 m, would tighten it by directly measuring the wind direction at both extremes.

I'm weighing a test drop at 150 m with a north heading, so that the aircraft's motion lines up with the crosswind component and the lateral drift shows up directly in the impact y-residual.

I'm working out the lateral sensitivity at 150 m: a 1-degree change in wind direction there shifts the landing y by roughly 1.6 m over a 12-second fall, which is enough to matter for the veer question.

I'm weighing the lateral sensitivity at 150 m: about 1.6 m of landing shift per degree of wind direction, which is close to the measurement noise, so three more drops should bring the veer estimate down to roughly 1 m of precision. At 30 m the same change barely moves the landing point, so the high-altitude drops are the ones worth spending.

I'm weighing whether to use the eighth drop at 150 m with a north heading and speed of 60, since the crosswind at that height gives the lateral residual the most leverage on the veer estimate. Drag will differ with that heading, but the model already accounts for it, so the drop should still add a useful data point.

I'm weighing a test drop at 150 m heading north, since the lateral sensitivity there is high enough to tighten the veer estimate, and I'll release from about (0, -200) so the drop clears the target area.

I'm comparing the two candidate settings: the one with veer -3.3 and direction 91.7 pulls the dy mean further negative, averaging about -1.1, while the 90.5 and -2 setting sits near -0.1, so the first looks better for dy. Next I'm checking the residuals for the 90.5, -2 setting, where the dy values average about -0.25.

Checking the remaining two test drops now: I'm weighing whether to use them to refine drag at 80 m/s, since the residuals there already look reasonable, or to replicate a run to cut down noise.

I'm thinking about running one more test drop at 80 m/s and altitude 40, heading west, to check speed dependence and drag, since the west heading would have the drop pass through the smoke with the east wind pushing against it.

I'm checking whether the residuals are small enough, which they are, so the model looks sound. Next I'm comparing two drag values, 0.037 and 0.039, to see which fits better overall. The mean dx is around 0.2, which seems fine to me. Then I'm moving on to the operation phase, where the targets get revealed, and I'll declare a calibration hypothesis with d=0.038, W=7.0 and dir=90.5.

I'm weighing whether to spend the last test drop before starting the operation, since once that begins no test is possible. The targets are far from the calibration fire, so the wind should be the same, and a test at 150 m could still firm up the veer estimate. I'll run it now and then move on.
I've settled on a final set of parameters: drag 0.038, wind 7.0, direction 90.5, shear 0.25, veer -2, updraft 3.6. I'll run two comparisons on nearby drag and updraft values to check the overall fit.

The drag at 0.0375 with updraft 3.6 looks good, since the dt residuals come out smaller. I'll lock in the final set: drag 0.0375, W 7.0, direction 90.5, shear 0.25, veer -2, and updraft 3.6. Next step is to move on to operation.

I'm working out, for each target, a heading, altitude, speed within range, and release point that make the impact land on it. To test a candidate I'm simulating with the target's updraft scaled by its intensity and the smoke, but the simulator doesn't take intensity directly, so I need to account for that somehow.

Since the simulator only places smoke at the origin, I'm planning to shift the release point by the negative of the target's position so the scene lines up, which works because the wind is uniform. The updraft is easy to scale by intensity, but the smoke radius also depends on intensity and the tool can't set that directly, so I'm weighing whether scaling the updraft alone is a close enough approximation.

I'm now going through the simulator's wind-drift numbers from earlier drops to estimate how far a release point at each height and heading will carry the load, starting from a no-updraft baseline and then correcting for the updraft.

I'm checking the remaining drop data against the impacts: the wind-driven displacement at 150 m, 60 m, and 40 m altitudes, and the offset from the origin. For target 1, heading near east (about 84) and 45–65 m altitude, I'd expect the wind to push the load roughly 6 m east at 55 m.

I'm estimating the fall time for a 55 m release, which comes out to about 5 seconds, and checking that against the earlier drops at similar altitudes. Wind-driven displacement will be the main factor, so I'll use the simulator to get the release point rather than doing the full calculation by hand.

I'm going to set each target's release so the simulator's smoke sits at the origin, by offsetting the release point by the negative of the target's position, since the wind is uniform. Then I'll pick a heading, altitude, and speed within range and check the resulting impact relative to the target.

I'm thinking about getting the displacement from release to impact by simulating from a point far from the smoke, where there's no updraft, and then adding the smoke's effect separately.

I'm settling on the release approach: simulate each target with the release offset by the negative of the target's position, so the smoke sits at the origin, then solve for the release point that puts the impact on the target.

I'm settling on a release that's offset by the negative of the target's position, so the simulator's smoke sits at the origin. I'll read the impact from that relative run, shift the release by the negative of that miss, and repeat two or three times until the impact lands on the target.

I'm checking whether the updraft scaling works with the simulator's fixed radius, and I'm treating the small radius difference as negligible. I'm also making sure each release point stays within the allowed drop ranges, and I'm accepting that the entry into the smoke is only approximately modeled.

I'm picking mid-range values for target 1 (heading 84, altitude 55 m, speed 67) since they keep wind and updraft effects moderate. Next I'll run a simulation with a release point offset by the negative of the estimated displacement.

I'm estimating the displacement from the drop altitude and heading, using the earlier drop data as a rough guide, and I'm going to start with a guessed offset of about 60 m east and 7 m north to run the simulator.

I'm estimating the vertical drift from the aircraft's north component, which should add a small positive offset. I'll start the trial run with the release point at (-60, 0) for heading 84, altitude 55 m, and speed 67, then see where the impact lands.

I'm checking the impact position relative to the release point, which puts the landing at about 92 m downrange. Fall time is around 5.9 s, and the wind plus aircraft contributions bring the estimate to roughly 57 m. Next I'm recomputing the relative offset from the impact point back to the release point.

I'm re-running the simulation with the release point shifted so the impact should land near the origin. I'll also note that the updraft term was set to 3.9, which comes from 3.6 times 1.09.

I'm working out the impact point at x = -2.3, so I need to shift the release position by +2.3 in x, which gives r ≈ (-90.1, -6.1). The smoke's updraft could shift things a bit, so I'm going to check that value quickly.

I've worked out the release point for the first target, offset by the wind drift, along with heading, altitude, and speed. I'm also checking how sensitive that result is to the smoke. Next I'm settling on values for the second target's heading, altitude, and speed within their ranges.

I'm picking a starting guess for the second target's release offset and running a rough simulation to see where the impact would land.

The displacement comes out to about (4.1, -29.6) from (200,130), which is small. Drag at 55 m/s would be enormous, around 113 m/s², so the aircraft's velocity dies within a second and the displacement must be coming mostly from the wind.

The wind's contribution looks like about 66 m eastward, yet the x-displacement comes out near 4, so the aircraft's leftover velocity must be pulling the load back.
